metadata.title: Justice Sotomayor signals support for Supreme Court term limits

sources.news_title: Liberal justice triggers once-indicted Trump ally with massive court shift tease
sources.text:
Justice Sonia Sotomayor's openness to Supreme Court term limits has drawn a lengthy rebuke from Jeffrey Clark, the former Trump Justice Department official who tried to help overturn the 2020 election.
Speaking at an event in Philadelphia on Friday, Sotomayor said she "wouldn't be unhappy with term limits," CNN reported. "We're the only country in the democratic world with lifetime appointments," she said.
Her comments come as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, which could give new life to proposals to reshape the high court.
Clark was not happy.
"With all due respect, that's an argument about comparative politics, not about what the Constitution actually says," Clark wrote on X Saturday. He argued that Article III's guarantee that judges "shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour" means life tenure, and that the only way to change it is a constitutional amendment.
He took aim at proposals to rotate justices off the bench after 18 years or move them into a "Senior Justice" role. Such plans, he said, would be "just converting life tenure into fixed terms and hoping nobody notices."
"Sorry, Ms. Justice, we've already noticed Senator Whitehouse's unconstitutional talk here brewing for years," he wrote, referring to Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), a leading advocate of court reform.
Clark also flagged the timing, pointing out that the push "is gaining steam at precisely the moment Democrats are poised to control both chambers of Congress, with Court expansion being discussed quite openly." He cited Justice Samuel Alito's recent warning of "a mounting campaign to change the direction of the Court's decisions by intimidating justices or, if that fails, by seriously damaging the Court's standing in the eyes of the public and then altering the Court's composition."
He then accused Sotomayor of self-interest. He argued that if reforms are adopted under Democratic control, "those who support her jurisprudential views will fill any new slots." "So she is also arguing for something to benefit herself without regard to the Constitution's text," he wrote.
Clark's criticism comes with heavy baggage. As acting head of the Justice Department's Civil Division in the final weeks of Trump's first term, he drafted a letter urging Georgia officials to reconsider the state's 2020 election results based on fraud concerns the department's own leadership rejected. Trump nearly installed him as acting attorney general before top DOJ officials threatened to resign en masse.
Clark was indicted alongside Trump in Georgia's sweeping election interference case, which was dismissed last year. He has also spent years fighting disbarment in Washington, D.C., where a bar disciplinary board recommended in 2025 that he lose his license.
Sotomayor's comments mark a shift in tone. In 2025, she expressed skepticism about how term limits could be applied to sitting justices, saying, "I am promised my job for life, and that can't be taken away constitutionally."

sources.news_title: Sotomayor Backs Supreme Court Term Limits as Dems Win
sources.text:
Justice Sonia Sotomayor told a Philadelphia audience she would not be unhappy with Supreme Court term limits, a push resurfacing as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
The court’s senior liberal justice spoke Friday at an event hosted by the American Philosophical Society and said term limits are an idea “being kicked around very actively.”
CNN reported that Sotomayor went further than a careful dodge. She told the room she could support limits on how long justices serve.
“As with everything else in life, I wouldn’t be unhappy with term limits,” Sotomayor said.
The timing is not subtle. Debate over structural changes at the Supreme Court has resurfaced after the Democratic midterm outcome, with Democrats set to take control of Congress next year. Lifetime tenure is written into the constitutional design for a reason: to keep justices independent of political pressure. Term-limit talk tends to spike when the left dislikes the Court’s recent direction.
Sotomayor’s comments came in a public setting, not a formal proposal on Capitol Hill. She answered questions and discussed recent high-profile decisions, including cases on birthright citizenship and presidential immunity.
US Circuit Judge David Tatel, who took senior status in 2022, asked whether the high court had lost something because most justices had taken similar professional paths to the bench. Sotomayor answered quickly.
"For sure,"
She added a sharper line about the work itself.
"They’ve forgotten that at the center of every case is people."
That is a justice’s critique of her own institution’s culture. It is not a drafted statute. And it does not erase the hard constitutional problem sitting underneath every term-limits pitch.
This is not the first time Sotomayor has weighed the idea out loud. In a 2024 appearance at the University of Zurich, she openly considered term limits and said a proposal could keep the Court’s ideological balance from being “skewed for too long.”
She also stated the obstacle that reformers prefer to soft-pedal. Federal judges are promised the job for life, she said, and “that can’t be taken away constitutionally.”
Audio from that appearance was later posted by Fix the Court, the watchdog group led by Gabe Roth. The clip matters because it shows the same justice holding two thoughts at once: openness to a political redesign, and recognition that the Constitution protects life tenure.
It remains far from clear whether Congress could impose term limits by ordinary law, or whether the move would require a constitutional amendment. That is not a technicality. It is the difference between a statute that can be flipped by the next majority and a permanent change to the founding charter.
Roth welcomed Sotomayor’s latest signal and framed public opinion as already settled in his direction.
"Even though poll after poll shows that most liberals and most conservatives support Supreme Court term limits, I don’t believe a majority of the current justices do, so it’s heartening to hear that Justice Sotomayor appears open to them,"
He did not stop at process. He went after the power of the office itself.
"After all, no one in a democracy should serve for 30 or 35 years, as has become the norm, in a position of such power, especially given the unbridled authority the Supreme Court has arrogated to itself this century."
That is the reform-left case in plain language: long service is the problem, and the Court’s authority is the target. The article notes term limits draw healthy support in public polling, though it does not name specific surveys or margins beyond Roth’s claim.
Even with Democrats taking Congress next year, the same report says it is unlikely such a measure would clear the Senate or win support from President Donald Trump. Justice Samuel Alito, for his part, has repeatedly stressed the importance of an independent judiciary since the election without diving into the details of these proposals.
Life tenure was not an accident of drafting. It was meant to wall off the Court from the election calendar, the donor class, and the mood of the moment. Once you put justices on a clock, you invite presidents and Senate majorities to time vacancies, shape benches, and treat the law as another spoils system.
Sotomayor’s Philadelphia line will be waved around as proof that “even a justice” sees the light. What she actually offered was softer than a formal endorsement of any specific plan, no length of term, no rule for sitting justices, no answer on statute versus amendment. She said she would not be unhappy. She also already said the constitutional promise of life tenure cannot simply be stripped away.
Democrats now heading into congressional control have every incentive to keep the pressure on a Court that has handed down major decisions they oppose. Republicans have every reason to treat the project as a power play dressed up as good-government hygiene.
A justice can float an idea at a society dinner in Philadelphia. Turning it into law still runs into the Constitution, the Senate, and a president who is not likely to sign off on shrinking the Court’s independence to please the party that just won a midterm.
When politicians come for life tenure, they are rarely chasing neutrality. They are chasing a different set of outcomes, and counting on voters not to notice the difference.

sources.news_title: Justice Sotomayor signals support for Supreme Court term limits
sources.text:
Justice Sonia Sotomayor told an audience in Philadelphia on Friday that she could support term limits for members of the Supreme Court, treading into a debate that may pick up steam when Democrats take control of Congress next year.
Sotomayor, the court’s senior liberal justice, noted that many other nations have managed to keep politics out of their judiciaries without lifetime appointments. After telling an audience that she wouldn’t offer an opinion on the idea, she then hinted that she was open to supporting the idea.
“As with everything else in life, I wouldn’t be unhappy with term limits,” Sotomayor said at an event hosted by the American Philosophical Society.
The discussion around proposed structural changes at the Supreme Court has resurfaced after the Democratic rout in the midterm election. Much of that debate has come from conservatives warning against ideas that have existed for years. Justice Samuel Alito, for instance, has repeatedly stressed the importance of an independent judiciary since the election, without getting into details about proposals.
Sotomayor noted in Philadelphia that term limits were an idea “being kicked around very actively.”
Term limits for justices receive healthy support in public opinion polling, though many Republicans view any change to the Supreme Court’s structure as an effort to undermine the judiciary’s independence. Even with Democratic control next year, it’s unlikely such a measure would clear the Senate or win support from President Donald Trump.
It’s also far from clear whether Congress could impose term limits by enacting a law, or whether such a move would require a far-harder-to-achieve constitutional amendment.
“Even though poll after poll shows that most liberals and most conservatives support Supreme Court term limits, I don’t believe a majority of the current justices do, so it’s heartening to hear that Justice Sotomayor appears open to them,” said Gabe Roth, who leads the Supreme Court watchdog Fix the Court.
“After all,” Roth said, “no one in a democracy should serve for 30 or 35 years, as has become the norm, in a position of such power — especially given the unbridled authority the Supreme Court has arrogated to itself this century.”
Sotomayor’s remarks appeared to go beyond what she said during an appearance at the University of Zurich in 2024 in which she openly weighed the idea. During that appearance, according to audio posted by Roth’s group, Sotomayor said the proposal would keep the ideological balance of the court from being “skewed for too long.”
But then she also suggested that federal judges are promised the job for life and “that can’t be taken away constitutionally.”
Much of Sotomayor’s remarks on Friday were focused on looking back at recent high-profile decisions from the court, including on birthright citizenship and presidential immunity. US Circuit Judge David Tatel, who took senior status in 2022, asked Sotomayor if the high court had lost something because most of its justices had taken similar professional paths to the bench.
“For sure,” Sotomayor said. “They’ve forgotten that at the center of every case is people.”
